walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: library functions

steps.text: This is a different program. 50 is typed in. Do the same steps with your program.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, 12)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, 12)
OUTPUT ROUND(Eggs / 12, 1)

steps.text: DIV gives the whole number of times. How many 12s fit into 50? 12 x 4 = 48, and 12 x 5 = 60 is too many.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, 12)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, 12)
OUTPUT ROUND(Eggs / 12, 1)
DIV(50, 12) = 4

steps.text: MOD gives what is left over: 50 - 48 = 2.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, 12)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, 12)
OUTPUT ROUND(Eggs / 12, 1)
MOD(50, 12) = 2

DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, 12)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, 12)
OUTPUT ROUND(Eggs / 12, 1)
50 / 12 = 4.1666...

steps.text: ROUND keeps 1 decimal place. The digit after the 1 is five or more, so 4.1 rounds up to 4.2. Now do yours.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, 12)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, 12)
OUTPUT ROUND(Eggs / 12, 1)
ROUND(4.1666, 1) = 4.2

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the search use a flag that starts as FALSE?Show the answer

Nothing has matched before the loop starts. The flag only changes when a value matches.

From Unit 1: linear search.

Codes already holds:

Index12345

3  Found <- FALSE
4  FOR Index <- 1 TO 5

7      ENDIF

11  ELSE

13  ENDIF

steps.label: 2.2: Data Types and Constants
steps.content:
Programming, Logic and Testing

2.2: Data Types and Constants

Year 8

  • Today: choose the right kind of variable for each value, and keep a fixed value in one place.
  • The big question: why must a program know what kind of value it holds?
Think → Pair → Share13, 13.5, "thirteen" and TRUE. Why might a computer keep these four values in different ways?Show the answer

They are different kinds of value. You can add 13 and 13.5, but not "thirteen". TRUE is only ever yes or no.

steps.label: What Is a Data Type?
steps.content:
What Is a Data Type?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: the program says DECLARE Age : INTEGER, then Age <- "thirteen". What happens? Why?Show the worked answer

The program stops on line 2.

Why? Age was declared for whole numbers only. "thirteen" is text. The error says: Age is declared as INTEGER but you tried to store a STRING ("thirteen") in it..

A data type says what kind of value a variable can hold.

DECLARE Age : INTEGER
DECLARE Town : STRING
  • You give each variable its data type when you DECLARE it.
  • The program then only lets in that kind of value.
  • The wrong kind of value stops the program with an error.

steps.label: Compare: INTEGER and REAL
steps.content:
Compare: INTEGER and REAL

Think → Pair → SharePredict: which program runs? Why does the other one stop?Show the worked answer

B runs and outputs 1.62. A stops on line 2.

Why? An INTEGER holds whole numbers only, and 1.62 has a decimal part. The error says: Height is an INTEGER and cannot hold 1.62.

A height in metres: 1.62.

A

DECLARE Height : INTEGER
Height <- 1.62
OUTPUT Height

B

DECLARE Height : REAL
Height <- 1.62
OUTPUT Height
  • INTEGER: a whole number, like 13, 0 or -4.
  • REAL: a number with a decimal part, like 1.62 or 9.5.

steps.label: Your Turn: INTEGER or REAL?
steps.content:
Your Turn: INTEGER or REAL?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the computer need to know if a number can have a decimal part?Show the answer

It stores and checks whole numbers and decimal numbers in different ways.

Choose the data type for each value.

items.prompt: The number of pupils in a class, like 28.
items.explain: You count pupils in whole numbers. There is never half a pupil.

items.prompt: A runner's time in seconds, like 12.85.
items.explain: A time can have a decimal part, so it needs a REAL.

steps.label: Compare: "13" and 13
steps.content:
Compare: "13" and 13

Think → Pair → SharePredict: which program outputs 14? Why can the other one not add 1?Show the worked answer

B outputs 14. A stops on line 3.

Why? "13" in quotes is text, not an amount. The error says: "+" needs two numbers.

A

DECLARE Age : STRING
Age <- "13"
OUTPUT Age + 1

B

DECLARE Age : INTEGER
Age <- 13
OUTPUT Age + 1
  • STRING: text in quotes, like "Hat Yai" or "13".
  • A STRING is kept as characters. You cannot do sums with it.

steps.label: BOOLEAN: Only TRUE or FALSE
steps.content:
BOOLEAN: Only TRUE or FALSE

Think → Pair → SharePredict: why is BOOLEAN a better data type for Passed than STRING?Show the worked answer

A BOOLEAN can only be TRUE or FALSE. With a STRING, a typing slip like "Ture" could get in, and an IF that checks for "TRUE" would miss it.

BOOLEAN: a value that can only be TRUE or FALSE, like Found in a linear search.

DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
DECLARE Passed : BOOLEAN
INPUT Mark
IF Mark >= 50 THEN
    Passed <- TRUE
ELSE
    Passed <- FALSE
ENDIF
OUTPUT Passed
  • 62 is typed in: the output is TRUE.
  • Passed <- "Yes" stops the program: "Yes" is not TRUE or FALSE.
  • Use BOOLEAN for a yes or no question: paid, locked, found.

steps.label: What Is a Constant?
steps.content:
What Is a Constant?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: what happens if a later line says TicketPrice <- 50? Why?Show the worked answer

The program stops on that line.

Why? TicketPrice is a CONSTANT, so its value cannot be changed while the program runs.

A constant is a value that is set once and never changes while the program runs.

CONSTANT TicketPrice <- 45
DECLARE Tickets : INTEGER
INPUT Tickets
OUTPUT Tickets * TicketPrice
  • Write CONSTANT, a name, <- and the value.
  • Put constants at the top of the program.
  • Every line can use it. No line can change it.

steps.label: Compare: A Typed Number or a Constant
steps.content:
Compare: A Typed Number or a Constant

Think → Pair → ShareThe price goes up to 50. How many lines must you change in A? In B? Why is B safer?Show the worked answer

A: 3 lines. B: 1 line.

Why safer? In A it is easy to miss one 45, and that line gives a wrong price. In B every line uses Price, so one change fixes them all. The name Price also says what 45 means.

A snack costs 45 baht. Both programs work out the cost of the snacks sold.

A: 45 typed in

DECLARE Monday : INTEGER
DECLARE Tuesday : INTEGER
INPUT Monday
INPUT Tuesday
OUTPUT Monday * 45
OUTPUT Tuesday * 45
OUTPUT (Monday + Tuesday) * 45

B: a constant

CONSTANT Price <- 45
DECLARE Monday : INTEGER
DECLARE Tuesday : INTEGER
INPUT Monday
INPUT Tuesday
OUTPUT Monday * Price
OUTPUT Tuesday * Price
OUTPUT (Monday + Tuesday) * Price

steps.label: Your Turn: Using a Constant
steps.content:
Your Turn: Using a Constant

Think → Pair → ShareWhy are constants written at the top of the program?Show the answer

They are easy to find and change there, and they are set before any line uses them.

1  CONSTANT PassMark <- 50
2  DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
3  INPUT Mark
4  IF Mark >= PassMark THEN
5      OUTPUT "Pass"
6  ELSE
7      OUTPUT "Try again"
8  ENDIF
Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Activity 2: The Right Types and a Constant
steps.content:
Activity 2: The Right Types and a Constant

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the drill type in new values every time?Show the answer

A program must work for any value it is given, not just one.

Write each program with the right data types. Some must use a constant. New values are typed in every time.

steps.label: Explain: Why Use a Constant?
steps.content:
Explain: Why Use a Constant?

Think → Pair → ShareWhat makes an explanation worth 2 marks?Show the answer

A point, then what it means for the program, joined with so.

items.prompt: A program uses the speed limit 90 in six places. Explain why the programmer should make the speed limit a constant.
items.modelAnswer: If the limit changes, only one line needs to change (1), so no place can be missed and every line uses the same value (1).
scheme: A change to the value is made in one place only / only one line to edit
So no use of it can be missed / every line uses the same value / fewer errors / the name says what 90 means

steps.label: Practice: Fix the Data Types
steps.content:
Practice: Fix the Data Types

Think → Pair → ShareWhy can the wrong data type stop a program that has no other mistakes?Show the answer

Each variable only lets in its own kind of value. One wrong type means one value is refused.

Ploy types in her name, 1.58 for her height in metres, and 4 visits. The program stops.

1  DECLARE Name : STRING
2  DECLARE Height : INTEGER
3  DECLARE Member : STRING
4  DECLARE Visits : INTEGER
5  INPUT Name
6  INPUT Height
7  INPUT Visits
8  Member <- TRUE
Total: 3 marks
